Maladaptive Strategies.value: go over and over why the event happened to me
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma

vignette:
At 54, Javier Morales had been running a small import business for years, and before that he had spent time abroad doing relief work in a war zone, an experience he rarely described in full. In the first sessions, what came through was not a polished account but a set of sharply felt moments that still seemed to sit just under the surface of ordinary life. He spoke about moving through damaged streets with other aid workers, the sense that danger was always nearby and could break open without warning. The memory that stayed closest to him was of being physically near other people when gunfire erupted. He remembered bodies pressed together in a rush for cover, the shock of hearing shots crack through the air, and the immediate certainty that the difference between being alive and dead could come down to where a person was standing in relation to someone else. Even now, what stood out to him was not only the noise but the closeness: the feeling of another person at his shoulder, the compressed space, the absence of room to move.

In the months after he returned to the United States, Javier found that certain moments unsettled him in ways he could not explain to his family. Loud popping sounds, a car backfiring in traffic, or anything resembling a gunshot could pull him up short before he had time to think. Just as troubling to him, though harder to explain, was what happened when life felt good. A celebratory dinner with his wife, laughter with friends, even the brief warmth of pride when his business had a strong month could suddenly feel wrong to him, almost dangerous. He had come to mistrust positive emotion itself. When he noticed himself relaxing or enjoying something, he became confused and tense, as if pleasure meant he was forgetting something essential or exposing himself to harm. He could not make those moments fit with what he knew about the world since the war zone, and the mismatch disturbed him.

Javier also became preoccupied with trying to make sense of why that deployment had happened to him. He described going over and over the same question—why me, why there, why was I the one who had to see that—and finding no answer that settled anything. These were not abstract reflections but repetitive loops that filled long drives, sleepless stretches, and quiet parts of the workday. At the office, while reviewing invoices or speaking with suppliers, he would catch himself circling back again to the same reasoning, trying to pin down a meaning that remained out of reach. He experienced this as urgent mental work, as though if he could finally explain it, something inside him would loosen.

Over time his habits changed in visible ways. He began carrying a weapon. He described this less as a political statement than as something that made immediate sense in his body; being unarmed felt intolerable, especially in public or when another person stood too close to him. In his role as a business owner, he was often in close quarters with employees, delivery drivers, and customers, and the ordinary physical proximity of business life became charged. If a driver stepped in close while discussing a shipment or a customer leaned toward his desk to point at paperwork, Javier felt his muscles tighten and his attention narrow. He preferred to position himself near exits, keep space around him, and know that the weapon was there.

His wife had also noticed another pattern that Javier himself recognized with some shame. At home and at work, he sometimes picked arguments or stirred up drama. A minor mistake by an employee could turn into a heated confrontation; a small disagreement at dinner could become a larger fight. He understood, at least in part, that conflict gave him somewhere to put the pressure building inside him. The charged feeling of an argument was easier for him to grasp than the older, more disorganizing fear that seemed to arrive out of nowhere. Still, this had taken a toll. Staff had begun to approach him cautiously, and his wife had started telling him that she never knew when the mood in the room would suddenly change.

By the time Javier sought help, he was exhausted by the narrowness of his life and by how little sense his reactions made to him, especially during moments that were supposed to be happy. What finally pushed him into treatment was not a single dramatic incident but the accumulation of them: flinching at sharp sounds, feeling alarmed when people came physically close, mistrusting his own enjoyment, going home and replaying again why the war had happened to him, and watching himself provoke one more unnecessary argument. He said he wanted to understand why he could not simply feel safe with his wife, in his business, in a good moment. What frightened him most was the sense that even peace and closeness had become things he could not trust, and what he hoped for was modest but deeply important to him: to stand near other people, hear a sudden noise, feel a moment of happiness, and not have his whole body act as if he were back there again.
